sp.p: Then it seems you would have told, if you had been trusted.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: O pox, Scandal, that was too far put. Never have told particulars, madam. Perhaps I might have talked as of a third person, or have introduced an amour of my own, in conversation, by way of novel, but never have explained particulars.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: But whence comes the reputation of Mr Tattle's secrecy, if he was never trusted?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Why thence it arises. The thing is proverbially spoken, but may be applied to him. As if we should say in general terms, he only is secret who never was trusted; a satirical proverb upon our sex. There's another upon yours: as she is chaste, who was never asked the question. That's all.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: A couple of very civil proverbs, truly. 'Tis hard to tell whether the lady or Mr Tattle be the more obliged to you. For you found her virtue upon the backwardness of the men, and his secrecy upon the mistrust of the women.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Gad, it's very true, madam, I think we are obliged to acquit ourselves. And for my part –But your ladyship is to speak first.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Am I? Well, I freely confess I have resisted a great deal of temptation.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: And egad, I have given some temptation that has not been resisted.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I cite Valentine here to declare to the court how fruitless he has found his endeavours, and to confess all his solicitations and my denials.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I am ready to plead not guilty for you, and guilty for myself.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: So, why this is fair. Here's demonstration with a witness.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Well, my witnesses are not present, but I confess I have had favours from persons. But as the favours are numberless, so the persons are nameless.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Pooh, pox, this proves nothing.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: No? I can shew letters, lockets, pictures and rings; and if there be occasion for witnesses, I can summon the maids at the chocolate houses, all the porters of Pall-Mall and Covent-Garden, the door-keepers at the Playhouse, the drawers at Locket's, Pontack's, the Rummer, Spring-Garden; my own landlady and valet de chambre, all who shall make oath that I receive more letters than the secretary's office, and that I have more vizor-masks to enquire for me than ever went to see the hermaphrodite or the naked prince. And it is notorious that in a country church once, an enquiry being made who I was, it was answered I was the famous Tattle, who had ruined so many women.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: It was there, I suppose, you got the nickname of the Great Turk.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: True: I was called Turk Tattle all over the parish. The next Sunday all the old women kept their daughters at home, and the parson had not half his congregation. He would have brought me into the Spiritual Court, but I was revenged upon him, for he had a handsome daughter whom I initiated into the science. But I repented it afterwards, for it was talked of in town. And a lady of quality that shall be nameless, in a raging fit of jealousy, came down in her coach and six horses and exposed herself upon my account. Gad, I was sorry for it with all my heart –you know whom I mean. You know where we raffled –

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Mum, Tattle.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: 'Sdeath, are not you ashamed?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: O barbarous! I never heard so insolent a piece of vanity. Fie, Mr Tattle, I'll swear I could not have believed it. Is this your secrecy?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Gadso, the heat of my story carried me beyond my discretion, as the heat of the lady's passion hurried her beyond her reputation. But I hope you don't know whom I mean; for there were a great many ladies raffled. Pox on't, now could I bite off my tongue.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No, don't; for then you'll tell us no more. Come, I'll recommend a song to upon the hint of my two proverbs, and I see one in the next room that will sing it.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: For Heavn's sake, if you do guess, say nothing. Gad, I'm very unfortunate.

div2.stage: Re-enter Scandal, with one to sing.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Pray sing the first song in the last new play.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Sampson, Mrs Frail, Miss Prue and Servant.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Is Ben come? Odso, my son Ben come? Odd, I'm glad on't. Where is he? I long to see him. Now, Mrs Frail, you shall see my son Ben. Body o' me, he's the hopes of my family. I ha'n't seen him these three years. I warrant he's grown. Call him in, bid him make haste. I'm ready to cry for joy.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Now, Miss, you shall see husband.

p.seg: Pish, he shall be none of my husband.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Hush. Well he shan't, leave that to me. I'll beckon Mr Tattle to us.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Won't you stay and see your brother?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: We are the twin stars, and cannot shine in one sphere; when he rises I must set. Besides, if I should stay, I don't know but my father in good nature may press one to the immediate signing the deed of conveyance of my estate, and I'll defer it as long as I can. Well, you'll come to a resolution.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I can't. Resolution must come to me, or I shall never have one.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Come, Valentine, I'll go with you; I've something in my head to communicate to you.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: What, is my son Valentine gone? What, is he sneaked off, and would not see his brother? There's an unnatural whelp! There's an ill-natures dog! What, were you here too, madam, and could not keep him? Could neither love, nor duty, nor natural affection oblige him? Odsbud, madam, have no more to say to him; he is not worth your consideration. The rogue has not a drachm of generous love about him. All interest, all interest. He's an undone scoundrel, and courts your estate. Body o' me, he does not care a doit for your person.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I'm pretty even with him, Sir Sampson; for if ever I could have liked anything in him, it should have been his estate too. But since that's gone, the bait's off, and the naked hook appears.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Odsbud, well spoken! And you are a wiser woman than I thought you were. For most young women nowadays are to be tempted with a naked hook.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: If I marry, Sir Sampson, I'm for a good estate with any man, and for any man with a good estate. Therefore if I were obliged to make a choice, I declare I'd rather have you than your son.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Faith and troth, you're a wise woman, and I'm glad to hear you say so. I was afraid you were in love with the reprobate. Odd, I was sorry for you with all my heart. Hang him, mungrel! Cast him off, you shall see the rogue shew himself, and make love to some desponding cadua of fourscore for sustenance. Odd, I love see a young spendthrift forced to cling to an old woman for support, like ivy round a dead oak, faith I do. I love to see 'em hug and cotton together, like down upon a thistle.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Where's father?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: There, sir, his back's toward you.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: My son Ben! Bless thee, my dear boy. Body o' me, thou art heartily welcome.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Thank you, father, and I'm glad to see you.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Odsbud, and I'm glad to see thee. Kiss me, boy, kiss me again and again, dear Ben.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: So, so, enough, father. Mess, I'd rather kiss these gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: And so thou shalt. Mrs Angelica, my son Ben.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Forsooth, an you please. [Salutes her.] Nay, mistress, I'm not for dropping anchor here. About ship, i'faith. [Kisses Mrs Frail.] Nay, and you too, my little cock-boat. So!

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Sir, you're welcome ashore.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Thank you, thank you, friend.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Thou hast been many a weary league, Ben, since I saw thee.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Ey, ey, been! Been far enough, an that be all. Well father, and how do all at home? How does brother Dick, and brother Val?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Dick? Body o' me, Dick has been dead these two years! I writ you word when you were at Legorne.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Mess, and that's true; marry I had forgot. Dick's dead, as you say. Well, and how? I have a many questions to ask you. Well, you be'nt married again, father, be you?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: No, I intend you shall marry, Ben. I would not marry for thy sake.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Nay, what does that signify? An you marry again, why then, I'll go to sea again, so there's one for t'other, an that be all. Pray don't let me be your hindrance. E'en marry a God's name an the wind sit that way. As for my part, mayhap I have no mind to marry.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: That would be pity, such a handsome young gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Handsome! He, he, he! Nay forsooth, an you be for joking, I'll joke with you, for I love my jest, an the ship were sinking, as we sayn at sea. But I'll tell you why I don't much stand towards matrimony. I love to roam about from port to port, and from land to land. I could never abide to be port-bound as we call it. Now a man that is married has as it were, d'ye see, his feet in the bilboes, and mayhap mayn't get 'em out again when he would.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ben's a wag.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: A man that is married, d'ye see, is no more like another man than a galley-slave is like one of us free sailors. He is chained to an oar all his life, and mayhap forced to tug a leaky vessel into the bargain.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: A very wag, Ben's a very wag. Only a little rough, he wants a little polishing.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Not at all. I like his humour mightily, it's plain and honest. I should like such a humour in a husband extremely.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Sayn you so forsooth? Marry and I should like such a handsome gentlewoman for a bed-fellow hugely. How say you, mistress, would you like going to sea? Mess, you're a tight vessel, and well rigged, an you were but as well manned.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: I should not doubt that, if you were master of me.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: But I'll tell you one thing, an you come to sea in a high wind, or that, lady, you mayn't carry so much sail o'your head. Top and top-gallant, by the Mess.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: No, why so?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why an you do, you may run the risk to be overset, and then you'll carry your keels above water, he, he, he!

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I swear, Mr Benjamin is the veriest wag in nature, an absolute sea-wit.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Nay, Ben has parts, but as I told you before, they want a little polishing. You must not take anything ill, madam.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: No, I hope the gentlewoman is not angry. I mean all in good part, for if I give a jest, I'll take a jest, and so forsooth you may be as free with me.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: No, I hope the gentlewoman is not angry. I mean all in good part, for if I give a jest, I'll take a jest, and so forsooth you may be as free with me.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I thank you, sir, I am not at all offended. But methinks, Sir Sampson, you should leave him alone with his mistress. Mr Tattle, we must not hinder lovers.

p.seg: Well, Miss, I have your promise.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Body o' me, madam, you say true. Look you, Ben, this is tour mistress. Come, Miss, you must not be shamefaced, we'll leave you together.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: I can't abide to be left alone. Mayn't my cousin stay with me?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: No, no. Come, let's away.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Look you, father, mayhap the young woman mayn't take a liking to me.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: I warrant thee, boy. Come, come, we'll be gone. I'll venture that.

div2.stage: Exeunt all but Ben and Miss Prue.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Come mistress, will you please to sit down? For an you stand a stern a that'n, we shall never grapple together. Come, I'll haul a chair. There, an you please to sit, I'll sit by you.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: You need not sit so near one. If you have anything to say, I can hear farther off, I an't deaf.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why, that's true as you say, nor I an't dumb; I can be heard as far as another. I'll heave off to please you. [Sits farther off.] An we were a league asunder, I'd undertake to hold discourse with you, an 'twere not a main high wind indeed, and full in my teeth. Look you forsooth, I am as it were bound for the land of matrimony. 'Tis a voyage d'ye see that was none of my seeking. I was commanded by father, and if you like of it, mayhap I may steer into your harbour. How say you, mistress? The short of the thing is this, that if you like me, and I like you, we may chance to swing in a hammock together.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: I don't know what to say to you, nor I don't care to speak with you at all.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: No? I'm sorry for that. But pray, why are you so scornful?

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: As long as one must not speak one's mind, one had better not speak at all, I think, and truly I won't tell a lie for the matter.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Nay, you say true in that, it's but a folly to lie. For to speak one thing and to think just the contrary way is, as it were, to look one way and to row another. Now for my part d'ye see, I'm for carrying things above board. I'm not for keeping anything under hatches. So that if you ben't as willing as I, say so a God's name, there's no harm done. Mayhap you may be shamefac'd. Some maidens, thof they love a man well enough, yet they don't care to tell'n so to's face. If that's the case, why, silence gives consent.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: But I'm sure it is not so, for I'll speak sooner than you should believe that. And I'll speak truth, tho' one should always tell a lie a man. And I don't care, let my father do what he will. I'm too big to be whipped, so I'll tell you plainly, I don't like you, nor love you at all, nor never will, that's more. So, there's your answer for you, and don't trouble me no more, you ugly thing.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Look you, young woman. You may learn to give good words, however. I spoke you fair, d'ye see, and civil. As for your love or your liking, I don't value it of a rope's end. And mayhap I like you as little as you do me. What I said was in obedience to father. Gad, I fear a whipping no more than you do. But I tell you one thing, if you should give such language at sea, you'd have a cat o' nine tails laid' cross your shoulders. Flesh, who are you? You heard t'other handsome young woman speak civilly to me, of her own accord. Whatever you think of yourself, Gad I don't think you are any more to compare to her than a can of small beer to a bowl of punch.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Well, and there's a handsome gentleman, and a fine gentleman, and a sweet gentleman, that was here that loves me, and I love him; and if he sees you speak to me any more, he'll thrash your jacket for you, he will, you great sea-calf.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: What, do you mean that fair-weather spark that was here just now? Will he thrash my jacket? Let'n, let'n. But an he comes near me, mayhap I may giv'n a salt eel for's supper for all that. What does father mean to leave me alone as soon as I come home with such a dirty dowdy? Sea-calf! I an't calf enough to lick your chalked face, you cheese-curd you. Marry thee! Ouns! I'll marry a Lapland with as soon, and wracked vessels.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: I won't be called names, nor I won't be abused thus, so I won't. If I were a man [cries.] you durst not talk at this rate. No you durst not, you stinking tar-barrel.

div2.stage: Enter Mrs Foresight and Mrs Frail.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: They have quarrelled just as we could wish.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Tar-barrel? Let your sweetheart there call me so, if he'll take your part, your Tom Essence, and I'll say something to him. Gad I'll lace his musk-doublet for him! I'll make him stink! He shall smell more like a weasel than a civet cat afore I ha'done with 'en.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Bless me, what's the matter, Miss? What, does she cry? Mr Benjamin, what have you done to her?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Let her cry: the more she cries, the less she'll –she has been gathering foul weather in her mouth, and now it rains out at her eyes.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Come, Miss, come along with me, and tell me, poor child.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Lord, what shall we do, there's my brother Foresight, and Sir Sampson coming. Sister, do you take Miss down into the parlour, and I'll carry Mr Benjamin into my chamber, for they must not know that they are fall'n out. Come, sir, will you venture yourself with me?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Venture? Mess, and that I will, tho' 'twere to sea in a storm.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: I left 'em together here. What, are they gone? Ben's a brisk boy. He has got her into a corner. Father's own son, faith, he'll touzle her, and mouzle her. The rogue's sharp set, coming from sea, if he should not stay for saving grace, old Foresight, but fall to without the help of a parson, ha? Odd, if he should I could not be angry with him. 'Twould be but like me, a chip of the old block. Ha! Thou'rt melancholy, old Prognostication, as melancholy as if thou hadst spilt the salt, or pared thy nails of a Sunday. Come, cheer up, look about thee. Look up, old star-gazer. Now is he poring upon the ground for a crooked pin, or an old horse-nail, with the head towards him.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Sir Sampson, we'll have the wedding tomorrow morning.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: At ten a clock, punctually at ten.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: To a minute, to a second. Thou shall set thy watch, and the bridegroom shall observe its motions. They shall be married to a minute, go to bed to a minute, and when the alarm strikes, they shall keep time like the figures of St Dunstan's clock, and consummatum est shall ring all over de parish.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Sir Sampson, sad news.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Bless us!

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Can't you guess at what ought to afflict you and him, and all of us, more than anything else?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Body o' me, I don't know any universal grievance but a new tax, and the loss of the Canary Fleet, without popery should be landed in the West, or the French fleet were at anchor at Blackwall.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No. Undoubtedly Mr Foresight knew all this, and might have prevented it.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: 'Tis no earthquake!

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No, no yet, nor whirlwind. But we don't know what it may come to. But it has had a consequence already that touches us all.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Why, body o' me, out with't.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Something has appeared to your son Valentine. He's gone to bed upon't, and very ill. He speaks little, yet says he has a world to say. Asks for his father and the wise Foresight; talk of Raymond Lully, and the ghost of Lilly. He has secrets to impart, I suppose, to you two. I can get nothing out of him but sighs. He desires he may see you in the morning, but would not be disturbed tonight, because he has some business to do in a dream.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Hoity toity, what have I to do with his dreams or his divination? Body o' me, this is a trick to defer signing the conveyance. I warrant the devil will tell in a dream that he must not part with his estate. But I'll bring him a parson to tell him that the devil's a liar. Or if that won't do, I'll bring a lawyer that shall out-lie the devil. And so I'll try whether my blackguard or his shall get the better of the day.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Alas, Mr Foresight, I'm afraid all is not right. You are a wise man, and a conscientious man, a searcher into obscurity and futurity, and if you commit an error, it is with a great deal of consideration, and discretion, and caution.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Ah, good Mr Scandal –

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Nay, nay, 'tis manifest; I do not flatter you. But Sir Sampson is hasty, very hasty. I'm afraid he is not scrupulous enough, Mr Foresight. He has been wicked, and heaven grant he may mean well in his affair with you. But my mind gives me, these things cannot be wholly insignificant. You are wise, and should not be overreached, methinks you should not –

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Alas, Mr Scandal – Humanum est errare.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: You say true, man will err, mere man will err; but you are something more. There have been wise men, but they were such as you, men who consulted the stars, and were observers of omens. Solomon was wise, but how? By his judgement in astrology. So says Pineda in his third book and eighth chapter.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: You are learned, Mr Scandal.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: A trifler, but a lover of art. And the wise men of the East owed their instruction to a star, which is rightly observed by Gregory the Great in favour of astrology. And Albertus Magnus makes it the most valuable science, because, says he, it teaches us to consider the causation of causes in the causes of things.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I protest I honour you, Mr Scandal. I did not think you had been read in these matters. Few young men are inclined –

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I thank my stars that have inclined me. But I fear this marriage and making over this estate, this transferring of a rightful inheritance, will bring judgements upon us. I prophesy it, and I would not have the fate of Cassandra, not to be believe. Valentine is disturbed; what can be the cause of that? And Sir Sampson is hurried on by an unusual violence. I fear he does not act wholly from himself; methinks he does not look as he used to do.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: He was always of an impetuous nature. But as to this marriage, I have consulted the stars; and all appearances are prosperous.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Come, come, Mr Foresight, let not the prospect of worldly lucre carry you beyond your judgement, nor against your conscience. You are not satisfied that you act justly.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: You are not satisfied, I say. I am loath to discourage you. But it is palpable that you are not satisfied.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How does it appear, Mr Scandal? I think I am very well satisfied.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Either you suffer yourself to deceive yourself, or you do not know yourself.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Pray explain yourself.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Do you sleep well o'nights?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Are you certain? You do not look so.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I am in health, I think.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: So was Valentine this morning, and looked just so.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How? Am I altered any way? I don't perceive it.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Thar may be, but your beard is longer that it was two hours ago.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Indeed? Bless me!

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Husband, will you go to bed? It's ten a clock. Mr Scandal, your servant.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: [aside] Pox on her, she has interrupted my design. But I must work her into the project. [Aloud] You keep early hours, madam.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Mr Foresight is punctual, we sit up after him.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: My dear, pray lend me your glass, your little looking-glass.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p:
Pray lend it him, madam. I'll tell you the reason. [She gives him the glass: Scandal and she whisper.]
My passion for you is grown so violent that I am no longer master of my self. I was interrupted in the morning, when you had charity enough to give me your attention, and I had hopes of finding another opportunity of explaining myself to you, but was disappointed all this day, and the uneasiness that has attended me ever since bring me now hither at this unseasonable hour.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Was there ever such impudence? To make love to me before my husband's face! I'll swear I'll tell him.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Do, I'll die a martyr rather than disclaim my passion. But come a little farther this way, and I'll tell you what project I had to get him out of the way, that I might have an opportunity of waiting upon you.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: [looking in the glass] I do not see any revolution here. Methinks I look with a serene and benign aspect –pale, a little pale– but the roses of these cheeks have been gathered many years. Ha! I do not like that suddain flushing. Gone already! Hem, hem, hem! Faintish. My heart is pretty good, yet it beats; and my pulses? Ha! I have none. Mercy on me! Hum. Yes, here they are. Gallop, gallop, gallop, gallop, gallop, gallop. Hey, whither will they hurry me? Now they're gone again, and now I'm faint again, and pale again, and hem! and my –hem? –breath, hem! –grows short. Hem, hem! He, he, hem!

p.seg: It takes. Pursue it in the name of love and pleasure.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: How do you do, Mr Foresight?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Hum, not so well as I thought I was. Lend me your hand.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Look you there now. Your lady says your sleep has been unquiet of late.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Very likely.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Oh, mighty restless, but I was afraid to tell him so. He has been subject to talking and starting.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: And did not use to be so?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Never, never, till within these three nights. I cannot say that he has once broken my rest since we have been married.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I will go to bed.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Do so, Mr Foresight, and say your prayers. He looks better than he did.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: [calls] Nurse, nurse!

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Do you think so, Mr Scandal?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Yes, yes, I hope this will be gone by morning, taking it in time.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I hope so.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Nurse, your master is not well; put him to bed.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I hope you will be able to see Valentine in the morning. You had best take a little diacodion and cowslip water, and lie upon your back. Maybe you may dream.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I thank you, Mr Scandal, I will. Nurse, let me have a watch-light, and lay the Crumbs of Comfort by me.

sp.speaker: Nurse
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: And – Hem, hem! I am very faint.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No, no, you look much better.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Do I? And d'ye hear, bring me, let me see, within a quarter of twelve –hem –he, hem! –just upon the turning of the tide, bring me the urinal. And I hope neither the lord of my ascendants not the moon will be combust, and then I may do well.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I hope so. Leave that to me; I will erect a scheme; and I hope I shall find both Sol and Venus in the sixth house.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I thank you, Mr Scandal. Indeed, that would be a great comfort to me. Hem, hem! Good night.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Good night, good Mr Foresight. And I hope Mars and Venus will be in conjunction while your wife and I are together.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Well, and what use do you hope to make of this project? You don't think that you are ever like to succeed in your design upon me?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Yes, faith, I do. I have a better opinion both of you and myself than to despair.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Did you ever hear such a toad? Hark'ee devil, do you think any woman honest?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Yes, several, very honest. They'll cheat a little at cards sometimes, but that's nothing.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Pshaw! but virtuous, I mean?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Yes, faith, I believe some women are virtuous too; but 'tis as I believe some men are valiant, thro' fear. For why should a man court danger, or a woman shun pleasure?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: O monstrous! What are conscience and honour?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Why, honour is a public enemy, and conscience a domestic thief; and he that would secure his pleasure must pay a tribute to one and go halves with the other. As for honour, that you have secured, for you have purchased a perpetual opportunity for pleasure.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: An opportunity for pleasure?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Ay, your husband, a husband is an opportunity for pleasure. So you have taken care of honour, and 'tis the least I can do to take care conscience.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: And so you think we are free for one another?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Yes faith, I think so. I love to speak my mind.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Why then, I'll speak my mind. Now as to this affair between you and me: Here you make love to me. Why, I'll confess it does not displease me. Your person is well enough and your understanding is not amiss.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I have no great opinion of myself, yet I think I'm neither deformed nor a fool.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: But you have a villainous character. You are a libertine in speech as well as practice.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Come, I know what you would say. You think it more dangerous to be seen in conversation with me than to allow some other men the last favour. You mistake; the liberty I take in talking is purely affected for the service of your sex. He that first cries out 'stop thief' is often he that has stolen the treasure. I am a juggler, that act by confederacy; and if you please, we'll put a trick upon the world.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Ay, but you are such an universal juggler that I'm afraid you have a great many confederates.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Faith, I'm sound.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: O fie, I'll swear you're impudent.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I'll swear you're handsome.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Pish, you'd tell me so, tho' you did not think so.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: And you'd think so, tho' I should not tell you so. And now I think we know one another pretty well.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: O Lord, who's here?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Mess, I love to speak my mind. Father has nothing to do with me. Nay, I can't say that neither, he has something to do with me. But what does that signify? If so be that I ben't minded to be steered by him, 'tis as thof he should drive against wind and tide.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Ay, but my dear, we must keep it secret till the state be settled. For, you know, marrying without an estate is like sailing in a ship without ballast.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: He, he, he! Why, that's true. Just so for all the world it is indeed, as like as two cable ropes.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: And tho' I have a good portion, you know one would not venture all in one bottom.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why, that's true again, for mayhap one bottom may spring a leak. You have hit it indeed, Mess, you've nick'd the channel.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Well, but if you should forsake me after all, you'd break my heart.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Break your heart? I'd rather the Mary-gold should break her cable in a storm, as well as I love her. Flesh, you don't think I'm false-hearted, like a land-man. A sailor will be honest, thof mayhap he has never a penny of money in his pocket. Mayhap I may not have so fair a face as a citizen or a courtier, but for all that I've as good in my veins, and a heart as sound as a biscuit.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: And will you love me always?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Nay, an I love once, I'll stick like pitch, I'll tell you that. Come I'll sing you a song of a sailor.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Hold, there's my sister. I'll her to hear it.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Well, I won't go to bed to my husband tonight, because I'll retire to my own chamber and think of what you have said.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Well, you'll give me leave to wait upon you to your chamber-door and leave you my last instructions?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Hold, here's my sister coming toward us.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: If it won't interrupt you, I'll entertain you with a song.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: The song was made upon one of our ship's crew's wife; our boatswain made the song. Mayhap you may know her, sir. Before she was married, she was called buxom Joan of Deptford.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I have heard of her.

lg.l: (sings: 1) A soldier and a sailor,
A tinker, and a tailor,
Had once a doubtful strife, sir,
To make a maid a wife, sir,
Whose name was buxom Joan.
For now the time was ended,
When she no more intended,
To lick her lips at men, sir,
And gnaw the sheers in vain, sir,
And lie o'nights alone.
The soldier swore like thunder,
He loved her more than plunder,
And shewed her many a scar, sir,
That he had brought from far, sir,
With fighting for her sake.
The tailor thought to please her,
With off'ring her this measure.
The tinker, too, with mettle,
Said he could mend her kettle,
And stop up ev'ry leak.
But while these three were prating,
The sailor slily waiting,
Thought if it came about, sir,
That they should all fall out, sir:
He then might pray his part.
And just e'en as he meant, sir,
To loggerheads they went, sir,
And then he let fly at her,
A shot 'twixt wind and water,
That won this fair maid's heart.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p:
If some of our crew that came to see me are not gone, you shall see that we sailors can dance sometimes, as well as other folks. [Whistles.] I warrant that brings 'em, an' they be within hearing. Enter Seamen.
Oh here they be, and fiddles along with 'em. Come my lads, let's have a round, and I'll make one. Dance.
We're merry folk, we sailors, we han't much to care for. Thus we live at sea; eat biscuit, and drink flip, put on a clean shirt once a quarter, come home and lie with our landladies once a year, get rid of a little money, and then put off with the next fair wind. How d'ye like us?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Oh, you are the happiest, merriest men alive.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: We're beholding to Mr Benjamin for this entertainment. I believe it's late.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why, forsooth, an you think so, you had best go to bed. For my part, I mean to toss a can and remember my sweetheart afore I turn in. Mayhap I may dream of her.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Mr Scandal, you had best go to bed and dream too.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Why, faith, I have a good lively imagination, and can dream as much to the purpose as another, if I set about it. But dreaming is the poor retreat of a lazy, hopeless, and imperfect lover. 'Tis the last glimpse of love to worn-out sinners, and the faint dawning of a bliss to wishing girls and growing boys.

lg.l: There's nought but willing, waking love that can
Make blest the ripened maid, and finished man.

div2.trailer: THE END OF THE THIRD ACT

div2.head: SCENE ONE

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Well, is your master ready? Does he look madly and talk madly?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Yes, sir, you need make no great doubt of that. He that was so near turning poet yesterday morning can't be much to seek in playing the madman today.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Would he have Angelica acquainted with the reason of his design?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: No sir, not yet. He has a mind to try whether his playing the madman won't make her play the fool and fall in love with him, or at least own that she has loved him all this while, and concealed it.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I saw her take coach just now with her maid, and think I heard her bid the coachman drive hither.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Like enough, sir, for I told her maid this morning my master was run stark mad only for love of her mistress. I hear a coach stop; if it should be she, sir, I believe he would not see her till he hears how she takes it.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Well, I'll try her. 'Tis she, here she comes.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Mr Scandal, I suppose you don't think it a novelty to see a woman visit a man at his own lodgings in a morning?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Not upon a kind occasion, madam. But when a lady comes tyrannically to insult a ruined lover, and make manifest the cruel triumphs of her beauty, the barbarity of it something surprises me.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I don't like raillery from a serious face. Pray tell me what is the matter.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: No strange matter, madam; my master's mad, that's all. I suppose your ladyship has thought him so a great while?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: How d'you mean, mad?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Why faith, madam, he's mad for want of his wits, just as he was (poor) for want of money. His head is e'en as light as his pockets, and anybody that has a mind to a bad bargain can't do better than to beg him for his estate.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: If you speak truth, your endeavouring at wit is very unseasonable.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Mr Scandal, you can't think me guilty of so much inhumanity as not to be concerned for a man I must own myself obliged to. Pray tell me truth.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Faith, madam, I wish telling a lie would mend the matter. But this is no new effect of an unsuccessful passion.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: [aside] I know not what to think –yet I should be vexed to have a trick put upon me. [Aloud] May I not see him?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I'm afraid the physician is not willing you should see him yet. Jeremy, go in and enquire.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Ha! I saw him wink and smile –I fancy 'tis a trick. I'll try. I would disguise to all the world a failing, which I must own to you. I fear my happiness depends upon the recovery of Valentine. Therefore I conjure you as you are his friend, and as you have compassion upon one fearful of affliction, to tell me what I am to hope for. I cannot speak, but you may tell me. Tell me, for you know what I would ask.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: [aside] So, this is pretty plain. [Aloud] Be not too much concerned, madam; I hope his condition is not desperate. An acknowledgement of love from you, perhaps, may work a cure, as the fear of your aversion occasioned his distemper.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: [aside] Say you so? Nay, then I'm convinced, and if I don't play trick for trick, may I never taste the pleasure of revenge. [Aloud] Acknowledgement of love! I find you have mistaken my compassion, and think me guilty of a weakness I am a stranger to. But I have too much sincerity to deceive you, and too much charity to suffer him to be deluded with vain hopes. Good nature and humanity oblige me to be concerned for him, but to love is neither in my power nor inclination, and if he can't be cured without I suck the poison from his wounds, I'm afraid he won't recover his sense till I lose mine.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Hey, brave woman, i'faith. Won't you see him, then, if he desire it?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: What signify a madman's desires? Besides, 'twould make me uneasy. If I don't see him, perhaps my concern for him may lessen. If I forget him, 'tis no more than he has done by himself; and now the surprise is over, methinks I am not half so sorry for him as I was.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: So, faith, good nature works apace; you were confessing just now an obligation to his love.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: But I have considered that passions are unreasonable and involuntary. If he loves, he can't help it, and if I don't love. I can't help it; no more than he can help his being a man, or I my being a woman; or no more than I can help my want of inclination to stay longer here. Come, Jenny.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Humh! An admirable composition, faith, this same womankind.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: What, is she gone, sir?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Gone? Why, she was never here, nor anywhere else, nor I don't know her if I see her, nor you neither.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Good lack! What's the matter now? Are any more of us to be mad! Why, sir, my master longs to see her, and is almost mad in good earnest with the joyful news of her being here.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: We are all under a mistake. Ask no questions, for I can't resolve you; but I'll inform your master. In the meantime, if our project succeed no better with his father than it does with his mistress, he may descend from his exaltation of madness into the road of commonsense and be content only to be made a fool with other reasonable people. I hear Sir Sampson. You know your cue; I'll to your master.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Sampson Legend with a Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: D'ye see, Mr Buckram, here's the paper signed with his own hand.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Good, sir. And the conveyance is ready drawn in this box, if he be ready to sing and seal.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ready? Body o' me, he must be ready. His sham sickness shan't excuse him. Oh, here's his scoundrel. Sirrah, where's your master?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Ah, sir, he's quite gone.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Gone! What, he is not dead?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: No, sir, not dead.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: What, is he gone out of town, run away, ha? Has he tricked me? Speak, varlet.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: No, no, sir, he's safe enough, sir, an he were but as sound, poor gentleman. He is indeed here, sir, and not here, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Hey-day, rascal, do you banter me? Sirrah, d'ye banter me? Speak, sirrah, where is he, for I will find him.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Would you could sir, for he has lost himself. Indeed, sir, I have a'most broke my heart about him. I can't refrain tears when I think of him, sir. I'm as melancholy for him as a passing-bell, sir, or a horse in a pound.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: A pox confound your similitudes, sir. Speak to be understood, and tell me in plain terms what the matter is with him, or I'll crack your fool's skull.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Ah, you've hit it, sir. That's the matter with him, sir. His skull's cracked, poor gentleman; he's stark mad, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Mad!

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: What, is he non compos?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Quite non compos, sir.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Why, then all's obliterated, Sir Sampson. If he be non compos mentis, his act and deed will be of no effect, it is not good in law.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ouns, I won't believe it. Let me see him, sir. Mad! I'll make him find his senses.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Mr Scandal is with him, sir; I'll knock at the door.

div2.stage: Goes to the scene, which opens and discovers Valentine upon a couch disorderly dressed, Scandal by him.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: How now, what's here to do?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: [starting] Ha! Who's that?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: For Heav'ns sake softly, sir, and gently. Don't provoke him.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Answer me. Who is that? And that?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Gads-bobs, does he not know me? Is he mischievous? I'll speak gently. Val, Val, dost thou not know me, boy? Not know thy own father, Val? I am thy own father, and this is honest Brief Buckram, the lawyer.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: It may be so. I did not know you. The world is full. These are people that we do know, and people that we do not know; and yet the sun shines upon all alike. There are fathers that have many children, and there are children that have many fathers. 'Tis strange! But I am truth, and come to give the world the lie.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Body o' me, I know not what to say to him.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Why does that lawyer wear black? Does he carry his conscience without-side? Lawyer, what art thou? Dost thou know me?

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: O Lord, what must I say? Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Thou liest, for I am truth. 'Tis hard, I cannot get a livelihood amongst you. I have been sworn out of Westminster Hall the first day of every term. Let me see –no matter how long –But I'll tell you one thing; it's a question that would puzzle an arithmetician, if you should ask him, whether the Bible saves more souls in Westminster Abbey, or damns more in Westminster Hall. For my part, I am truth, and can't tell; I have very few acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Body o' me, he talks sensibly in his madness. Has he no intervals?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Very short, sir.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Sir, I can do you no service while he's in this condition. Here's your paper, sir. He may do me a mischief if I stay. The conveyance is ready, sir, if he recover his senses.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Hold, hold, don't you go yet.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: You'd better let him go, sir, and send for him if there be occasion, for I fancy his presence provokes him more.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Is the lawyer gone? 'Tis well, then we may drink about without going together by the ears. Heigh ho! What a clock is't? My father here? Your blessing, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: He recovers. Bless thee, Val. How dost thou do, boy?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Thank you, sir, pretty well. I have been a little out of order. Won't you please to sit, sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ay, boy. Come, thou shalt sit down by me.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Sir, 'tis my duty to wait.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: No, no; come, come, sit you down, honest Val, How dost thou do? Let me feel thy pulse. Oh, pretty well now, Val. Body o' me, I was sorry to see thee indisposed. But I'm glad thou'rt better, honest Val.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Let me feel thy hand again, Val. It does not shake. I believe thou canst write, Val. Ha, boy? Thou can'st write name, Val? [In whisper to Jeremy] Jeremy, step and overtake Mr Buckram, bid him make haste black with the conveyance. Quick, quick!

p.seg: That ever I should suspect such a heathen of any remorse!

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Dost thou know this paper, Val? I know thou'rt honest, and wilt perform articles.

div2.stage: Shews him the paper, but holds it out of his reach.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Pray let me see it, sir. You hold it so far off that I can't tell whether I know it or no.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: See it, boy? Ay, ay, why thou dost see it. 'Tis thy own hand, Val. Why let me see, I can read it as plain as can be. Look you here: [reads] The condition of this obligation – Look you, as plain as can be, so it begins. And then at the bottom, as witness my hand, Valentine Legend, in great letters. Why, 'tis as plain as the nose in one's face. What, are my eyes better than thine? I believe I can read it farther off yet. Let me see.

div2.stage: [Stretches his arm as far as he can.]

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Will you please to let me hold it, sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Let thee hold it, say'st thou? Ay, with all my heart. What matter is it who holds it? What need anybody hold it? I'll put it put in my pocket, Val. And then nobody need hold it. [Puts the paper in his pocket.] There, Val: it's safe enough, boy. But thou shalt have it as soon as thou hast ser thy hand to another paper, little Val.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: What, is my bad genius here again? On no, 'tis the lawyer with an itching palm, and he's come to be scratched. My nails are not long enough. Let me have a pair of red-hot tongs quickly, quickly, and you shall see me act St Dunstan, and lead the devil by the nose.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: O Lord, let me be gone; I'll not venture myself with a madman.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! You need not run so fast, honesty will not overtake you. Ha, ha, ha! The rogue found me out to be in forma pauperis presently.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ouns! What a vexation is here! I know not what to do or say, nor which way to go.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Who's that, that's out of his way? I am truth, and can set him right. Hearkee, friend, the straight road is the worst way you can go. He that follows his nose always will very often be led into a stink. Probatum est. But what are you for? Religion or politics? There's a couple of topics for you, no more like one another than oil and vinegar. And yet those two beaten together by a state-cook make sauce for the whole nation.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: What the devil had I to do, ever to beget sons! Why did I ever marry?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Because thou wert a monster, old boy. The two greatest monsters in the world are a man and a woman. What's thy opinion?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Why, my opinion is that those two monsters joined together make yet a greater, that's a man and his wife.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Aha! Old truepenny, say'st thou so? Thou hast nick'd it. But it's wonderful strange, Jeremy!

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: What is, sir?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: That grey hairs should cover a green head –and I make a fool of my father.

div2.stage: Enter Foresight, Mrs Foresight, and Frail.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: What's here! Erra Pater? Or a bearded sybil? If prophecy comes, truth must give place.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: What says he? What, did he prophesy? Ha, Sir Sampson, bless us! How are we?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Are we? A pox o'your prognostication. Why, we are fools as we use to be. Ouns, that you could not foresee that the moon would predominate; and my son be mad. –Where's your oppositions, your trines, and your quadrates? What did you Cardan and your Ptolomee tell you? Your Messahalah and your Longomontanus, your harmony of chiromancy with astrology? Ah! pox on't, that I that know the world, and men and manners, that don't believe a syllable in the sky and stars, and sun and almanacs, and trash, should be directed by a dreamer, an omen-hunter, and defer business in expectation of a lucky hour. When, body o' me, there never was a lucky hour after the first opportunity.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Ah, Sir Sampson, heaven help your head. This is none of your lucky hour; nemo omnibus horis sapit. What, is he gone, and in contempt of science? Ill stars and unconverted ignorance attend him!

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: You must excuse his passion, Mr Foresight, for he has been heartily vexed. His son is non compos mentis, and thereby incapable of making any conveyance in law, so that all his measures are disappointed.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Ha! say you so?

p.seg: What, has my sea lover lost his anchor of hope then?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Oh, sister, what will you do with him?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Do with him? Send him to sea again in the next foul weather. He's used to an inconstant element, and won't be surprised to see the tide turned.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: [considers] Wherein was I mistaken, not to foresee this?

p.seg: Madam, you and I can tell him something else that he did not foresee, and more particularly relating to his own fortune.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: What do you mean? I don't understand you.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Hush, softy. The pleasures of last night, my dear, too considerable to be forgot so soon.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Last night! And what would your impudence infer from last night? Last night was like the night before, I think.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: 'S'death, do you make no difference between me and your husband?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Not much; he's superstitious, and you are mad, in my opinion.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: You make me mad. You are not serious. Pray recollect yourself.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Oh, yes, now I remember. You were very impertinent and impudent, and would have come to bed with me.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: And did not?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Did not! With that face can you ask the question?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: (aside) This I have heard of before, but never believed. I have been told she had that admirable quality of forgetting to a man's face in the morning that she had lain with him all night, and denying favours with more impudence than she could grant 'em. (Aloud) Madam, I'm your humble servant, and honour you. You look pretty well, Mr Foresight. How did you rest last night?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Truly Mr Scandal, I was so taken up with broken dreams and distracted visions that I remember little.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: 'Twas a very forgetting night. But would you not talk with Valentine? Perhaps you may understand him. I'm apt to believe there is something mysterious in his discourses, and sometimes rather think him inspired than mad.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: You speak with singular good judgement, Mr Scandal, truly. I am inclining to your Turkish opinion in this matter, and do reverence a man whom the vulgar think mad. Let us go in to him.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Sister, do you stay with them; I'll find out my lover and give him his discharge, and come to you. O' my conscience, here he comes.

div2.stage: Exeunt Foresight, Mrs Foresight and Scandal.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: All mad, I think. Flesh, I believe all the calentures of the sea are come ashore, for my part.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Mr Benjamin in choler?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: No, I'm pleased well enough, now I have found you. Mess, I've had such a hurricane upon your account yonder.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: My account? Pray, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why, father came and found me squabbling with yon chitty-faced thing, as he would have me marry, so he asked what was the matter. He asked in a surly sort of a way. It seems brother Val is gone mad, and so that put'n into a passion; but what, did I know that, what's that to me? So he asked in a surly sort of manner, and gad, I answered'n as surlily. What thof he be my father, I an't bound prentice to 'n. So, faith I told'n in plain terms, if I were minded to marry, I'd marry to please myself, not him. And for the young woman that he provided for me, I thought it more fitting for her to learn her sampler, and make dirt-pies, than to look after a husband. For my part I was none of her man. I had another voyage to make, let him take it as he will.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: So then you intend to go to sea again?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Nay, nay, my mind run upon you, but I would not tell him so much. So he said he'd make my heart ache, and if so be that he could get a woman to his mind, he'd marry himself. Gad, says I, an you play the fool and marry at these years, there's more danger of your head's aching than my heart. He was woundy angry when I gav'n that wipe. He hadn't a word to say, and so I left'n, and the green girl together. Mayhap the bee may bite, and he'll marry her himself, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: And were you this undutiful and graceless wretch to your father?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Then why was he graceless first? If I am undutiful and graceless, why did he beget me so? I did not get myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: O Impiety! How have I been mistaken! What an inhumane merciless creature have I set my heart upon? Oh, I am happy to have discovered the shelves and quicksands that lurk beneath that faithless smiling face.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Hey toss! What's the matter now? Why, you ben't angry, be you?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Oh, see me no more, for thou wert born amongst rocks, suckled by whales, credled in a tempest, and whistled to by winds; and thou art come forth with fins and scales, and three rows of teeth, a most outrageous fish of prey.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: O Lord, O Lord, she's mad, poor young woman. Love has turned her senses, her brain is quite overset. Well-a-day, how shall I do to set her to rights?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: No, no, I am not mad, monster, I am wise enough to find you out. Hadst thou the impudence to aspire at being a husband with that stubborn and disobedient temper? You that know not how to submit to a father, presume to have a sufficient stock of duty to undergo a wife? I should have been finely fobbed indeed, very finely fobbed.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Harkee, forsooth. If so be that you are in your right senses, d'ye see, for ought as I perceive I'm like to be finely fobbed, if I have got anger here upon your account, and you are tacked about already. What d'ye mean, after all your fair speeches, and stroking my cheeks, and kissing and hugging, what, would you sheer off so? Would you, and leave me aground?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: No, I'll leave you adrift, and go which way you will.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: What, are you false-hearted then?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Only the wind's changed.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: More shame for you! The wind's changed? It's an ill wind blows nobody good. Mayhap I have good riddance on you, if these be your tricks. What d'ye mean all this while, to make a fool of me?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Any fool, but a husband.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Husband! Gad I would not be your husband if you would have me, now I know your mind, thof you had your weight in gold and jewels, and thof I loved you never so well.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Why, canst thou love, porpoise?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: No matter what I can do, don't call names. I don't love you so well as to bear that, whatever I did. I'm glad you shew yourself, mistress. Let them marry you as don't know you. Gad, I know you too well, by sad experience. I believe he that marries you will go to sea in a hen-pecked frigate –I believe that, young woman– and mayhap may come to an anchor at Cuckold's Point. So there's a dash for you, take it as you will. Mayhap you may holla after me when I won't come too.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! No doubt on't.

lg.l: My true love is gone to sea. –

sp.p: O sister, had you come a minute sooner, you would have seen the resolution of a lover. Honest Tar and I are parted; and with the same indifference that we met. O' my life, I am half vexed at the insensibility of a brute that I despised.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: What then, he bore it most heroically?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Most tyrannically, for you see he has got the start of me, and I, the poor forsaken maid, am left complaining on the shore. But I'll tell you a hint that he has given me. Sir Sampson is enraged, and talks desperately of committing matrimony himself. If he has a mind to throw himself away, he can't do it more effectually than upon me, if we could bring it about.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Oh, hang him old fox, he's too cunning; besides, he hates both you and me. But I have a project in my head for you, and I have gone a good way towards it. I have almost made a bargain with Jeremy, Valentine's man, to sell his master to us.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Sell him, how?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Valentine raves upon Angelica, and took me for her, and Jeremy says will take anybody for her that he imposes on him. Now I have promised him mountains if in one of his mad fits he will bring you to him in her stead, and get you married together, and put to bed together; and after consummation, girl, there's no revoking. And if he should recover his senses, he'll be glad at least to make you a good settlement. Here they come, stand aside a little, and tell me how you like the design.

div2.stage: Enter Valentine, Scandal, Foresight, and Jeremy.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: [to Jeremy] And have you given your master a hint of their plot upon him?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Sir, sir; he says he'll favour it, and mistake her for Angelica.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: It may make sport.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Mercy on us!

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Husht. Interrupt me not. I'll whisper prediction to thee, and thou shalt prophesy. I am truth, and can teach thy tongue a new trick. I have told thee what's past; now I tell what's to come. Dost thou know what will happen tomorrow? Answer me not, for I will tell thee. Tomorrow, knaves will thrive thro' craft, and fools thro' fortune; and honesty will go as it did, frost-nipped in a summer suit. Ask me questions concerning tomorrow.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Ask him, Mr Foresight.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Pray what will be done at court?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Scandal will tell you. I am truth, I never come there.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: In the city?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Oh, prayers will be said in empty churches at the usual hours. Yet you will see such zealous faces behind counters, as if religion were to be sold in every shop. Oh, things will go methodically in the city, the clocks will strike twelve at noon, and the horned herd buzz in the Exchange at two. Wives and husbands will drive distinct trades, and care and pleasure separately occupy the family. Coffeehouses will be full of smoke and stratagem. And the cropped prentice, that sweeps his master's shop in the morning, may, ten to one, dirty his sheets before night. But there are two things that you will see very strange; which are wanton wives, with their legs at liberty, and tame cuckolds, with chains about their necks. But hold, I must examine you before I go farther, you look suspiciously. Are you a husband?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I am married.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Poor creature! Is your wife of Covent-Garden parish?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: No. St Martins-in-the-Fields.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Alas, poor man! His eyes are sunk, and his hands shrivelled, his legs dwindled, and his back bowed. Pray, pray, for a metamorphosis. Change thy shape, and shake off age; get thee Medea's kettle, and be boiled anew, come forth with lab'ring callous hands, a chine of steel, and Atlas shoulders. Let Taliacotus trim the calves of twenty chairmen, and make thee pedestals to stand erect upon, and look matrimony in the face. Ha, ha, ha! That a man should have a stomach to a wedding supper, when the pigeons ought rather to be laid to his feet, ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: His frenzy is very high now, Mr Scandal.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I believe it is a spring tide.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Very likely, truly. You understand these matters, Mr Scandal. I shall be very glad to confer with you about these things which he has uttered. His sayings are very mysterious and hieroglyphical.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Oh, why would Angelica be absent from my eyes so long?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: She's here, sir.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Now, sister.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: O Lord, what must I say?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Humour him, madam, by all means.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Where is she? Oh, I see her. She comes, like riches, health, and liberty at once, to a despairing, starving, and abandoned wretch. Oh, welcome, welcome.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: How de'e you, sir? Can I serve you?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Harkee; I have a secret to tell you. Endymion and the moon shall meet us upon Mount Latmos, and we'll be married in the dead of night. But say not a word. Hymen shall put his torch into a dark lanthorn, that it may be secret; and Juno shall give her peacock poppy-water, that he may fold his ogling tail, and Argus's hundred eyes be shut, ha? Nobody shall know, but Jeremy.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: No, no, we'll keep it secret. It shall be done presently.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: The sooner the better. Jeremy, come hither; closer, that none may overhear us. Jeremy, I can tell you news. Angelica is turned nun, and I am turning friar, and yet we'll marry one another in spite of the Pope. Get me a cowl and beads, that I may play my part, for she'll meet me two hours hence in black and white, and a long veil to cover the project, and we won't see one another's faces, till we have done something to be ashamed of; and then we'll blush once for all.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: I'll take care, and –

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Whisper.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Nay, Mr Tattle, if you make love to me you spoil my design, for I intended to make you my confidant.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: But, madam, to throw away your person –such a person!– and such a fortune, on a madman!

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I never loved him till he was mad; but don't tell anybody so.

p.seg: How's this? Tattle making love to Angelica!

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Tell, madam? Alas, you don't know me. I have much ado to tell your ladyship how long I have been in love with you. But encouraged by the impossibility of Valentine's making any more addresses to you, I have ventured to declare the very inmost passion of my heart. Oh madam, look upon us both. There you see the ruins of a poor decayed creature. Here, a complete and lively figure, with youth and health, and all his five senses in perfection, madam, and to all this, the most passionate lover –

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: O fie, for shame, hold your tongue. A passionate lover, and five senses in perfection! When you are as mad as Valentine, I'll believe you love me, and the maddest shall take me.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: It is enough. Ha, who's here?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: [to Jeremy] O Lord, her coming will spoil all.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: No, no, madam, he won't know her; if he should, I can persuade him.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: [whispers] Scandal, who are all these? Foreigners? If they are, I'll tell you what I think. Get away all the company but Angelica, that I may discover my design to her.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: (whispers) I will. I have discovered something of Tattle, that is of a piece with Mrs Frail. He courts Angelica. If we could contrive to couple 'em together. –Heark'ee –

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: He won't know you, cousin, he knows nobody.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: But he knows more than anybody. O niece, he knows things past and to come, and all the profound secrets of time.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Look you, Mr Foresight, it is not my way to make many words of matters, and so I shan't say much, but in short, d'ye see, I will hold you a hundred pound now that I know more secrets that he.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How? I cannot read that knowledge in your face, Mr Tattle. Pray, what do you know?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Why, d'ye think I'll tell you, sir? Read it in my face? No, sir, 'tis written in my heart. And safer there, sir, than letters writ in juice of lemon, for no fire can fetch it out. I am no blab, sir.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: [to Scandal] Acquaint Jeremy with it, he may easily bring it about. They are welcome, and I'll tell 'em so myself. (Aloud) What, do you look strange upon me? Then I must be plain. [Coming up to them.] I am truth, and hate an old acquaintance with a new face.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Do you know me, Valentine?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: You? Who are you? No, I hope not.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: I am Jack Tattle, your friend.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: My friend, what to do? I am no married man, and thou canst not lie with my wife; I am very poor, and thou canst not borrow money of me. Then what employment have I for a friend?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Hah! A good open speaker, and not to be trusted with a secret.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Do you know me, Valentine?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Oh, very well.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Who am I?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: You're a woman; one to whom heaven gave beauty, when it grafted roses on a briar. You are the reflection of heaven in a pond, and he that leaps at you is sunk. You are all white, a sheet of lovely spotless paper, when you first are born; but you are to be scrawled and blotted by every goose's quill. I know you; for I loved a woman, and loved her so long, that I found out a strange thing: I found out what a woman was good for.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay, prithee, what's that?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Why, to keep a secret.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: O Lord!

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: O exceeding good to keep a secret. For tho' she should tell, yet she is not to be believed.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Hah! Good again, faith.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I would have music. Sing me the song that I like.

lg.l: I tell thee, Charmion, could I time retrieve,
And could again begin to love and live,
To you I should my earliest off' ring give;
I know my eyes would lead my heart to you,
And I should all my vows and oaths renew,
But to be plain, I never would be true.
For by our weak and weary truth, I find,
Love hates to centre in a point assigned,
But runs with joy the circle of the mind.
Then never let us chain what should be free,
But for relief of either sex agree,
Since women love to change, and so do we.

sp.p: No more, for I am melancholy.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: [to Scandal] I'll do't, sir.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Mr Foresight, we had best leave him. He may grow outrageous, and do mischief.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I will be directed by you.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: [to Mrs Frail] You'll meet, Madam; I'll take care everything shall be ready.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Thou shalt do what thou wilt, have what thou wilt; in short, I will deny thee nothing.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: [to Angelica] Madam, shall I wait upon you?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: No, I'll stay with him. Mr Scandal will protect me. Aunt, Mr Tattle desires you would give him leave to wait on you.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: (aside) Pox on't, there's no coming off, now she has said that. (Aloud) Madam, will you do me the honour?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Mr Tattle might have used less ceremony.

div2.stage: Exeunt Foresight, Mrs Foresight, Tattle, Mrs Frail, Jeremy.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Jeremy, follow Tattle.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Mr Scandal, I only stay till my maid comes, and because I had a mind to be rid of Mr Tattle.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Madam, I am very glad that I overheard a better reason, which you gave to Mr Tattle; for his impertinence forced you to acknowledge a kindness for Valentine, which you denied to all his sufferings and my solicitations. So I'll leave him to make use of the discovery, and your ladyship to the free confession of your inclinations.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: O heavens! You won't leave me alone with a madman?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No, madam; I only leave a madman to his remedy.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Madam, you need not be very much afraid, for I fancy I begin to come to myself.

p.seg: Ay, but if I don't fit you, I'll be hanged.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: You see what disguises love makes us put on. Gods have been in counterfeited shapes for the same reason; and the divine part of me, my mind, has worn this mask of madness, and this motley livery only as the slave of love, and menial creature of your beauty.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Mercy on me, how he talks! Poor Valentine!

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Nay, faith, now let us understand one another, hypocrisy apart. The comedy draws toward an end, and let us think of leaving acting, and be ourselves; and since you have loved me, you must own I have at length deserved you should confess it.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: [sighs] I would I had loved you, for Heaven knows I pity you; and could I have foreseen the sad effects, I would have striven. But that's too late.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: What sad effects? What's too late? My seeming madness has deceived my father, and procured me time to think of means to reconcile me to him, and preserve the right of my inheritance to his estate, which otherwise, by articles, I must this morning have resigned. And this I had informed you of today, but you were gone before I knew you had been here.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: How? I thought your love of me had caused this transport in your soul, which it seems you only counterfeited for by mercenary ends and sordid interest.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Nay, now you do me wrong, for if any interest was considered, it was yours, since I thought I wanted more than love to make me worthy of you.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Then you thought me mercenary. But how am I deluded by this interval of sense, to reason with a madman?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Oh, 'tis barbarous to misunderstand me longer.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Oh, here's a reasonable creature; sure he will not have the impudence to persevere. Come, Jeremy, acknowledge your trick, and confess your master's madness counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Counterfeit, madam? I'll maintain him to be as absolutely and substantially mad as any freeholder in Bethlehem. Nay, he's as mad as any projector, fanatic, chymist, lover, or poet in Europe.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Sirrah, you lie. I am not mad.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! You see, he denies it.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: O Lord, madam, did you ever know any madman mad enough to own it?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Sot, can't you apprehend?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Why, he talked very sensibly just now.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Yes, madam, he has intervals: but you see he begins to look wild again now.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Why, you thick-skulled rascal, I tell you the farce is done, and I will be mad no longer.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! Is he mad or no, Jeremy?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p:
Partly, I think, for he does not know his mind two hours. I'm sure I left him just now in a humour to be mad. And I think I have not found him very quiet at this present.
[One knocks.] Who's there?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p:
Go see, you sot. [Exit Jeremy.]
I'm very glad that I can move your mirth, tho' not your compassion.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I did not think you had apprehension enough to be exceptious. But madmen shew themselves most by overpretending to a sound understanding, as drunken men do by over-acting sobriety. I was half inclining to believe you, till I accidentally touched upon your tender part. But now you have restored me to my former opinion and compassion.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Sir, your father has sent to know if you are any better yet. Will you please to be mad, sir, or how?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Stupidity! You know the penalty of all I'm worth must pay for the confession of my senses. I'm mad, and will be mad to everybody but this lady.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: So: just the very backside of truth. But lying is a figure in speech that interlards the greatest part of my conversation. Madam, your ladyship's woman.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Well, have you been there? Come hither.

p.seg: Yes, madam, Sir Sampson will wait upon you presently.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: You are not leaving me in this uncertainty?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Would anything but a madman complain of uncertainty? Uncertainty and expectation are the joys of life. Security is an insipid thing, and the overtaking and possessing of a wish discovers the folly of the chase. Never let us know one another better, for the pleasure of a masquerade is done when we come to shew faces. But I'll tell you two things before I leave you. I am not the fool you take me for, and you are mad and don't know it.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: From a riddle you can expect nothing but a riddle. There's my instruction and the moral of my lesson.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: What, is the lady gone again, sir? I hope you understood one another before she went.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Understood! She is harder to be understood than a piece of Egyptian antiquity, or an Irish manuscript; you may pore till you spoil your eyes, and not improve your knowledge.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: I have heard 'em say, sir, they read hard Hebrew books backwards; maybe you begin to read at the wrong end.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: They say so of a witches' prayer, and dreams and Dutch almanacks are to be understood by contraries. But there's regularity and method in that. She is a medal without a reverse or inscription, for indifference has both sides alike. Yet while she does nor seem to hate me, I will pursue her, and know her if it be possible, in spite of the opinion of my satirical friend, Scandal, who says,

lg.l: That women are like tricks by slight of hand,
Which, to admire, we should not understand.

div2.trailer: THE END OF THE FOURTH ACT

div2.head: SCENE ONE

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Where is Sir Sampson? Did you not tell me he would be here before me?

sp.speaker: Jenny
sp.p: He's at the great glass in the dining-room, madam, setting his cravat and wig.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: How! I'm glad on't. If he has a mind I should like him, it's a sign he likes me; and that's more than half my design.

sp.speaker: Jenny
sp.p: I hear him, madam.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Leave me, and d'ye hear, if Valentine should come or send, I am not to be spoken with.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: I have not been honoured with the commands of a fair lady a great while. Odd, madam, you have revived me; not since I was five and thirty.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Why, you have no great reason to complain, Sir Sampson, that is not long ago.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Zooks, but it is, madam, a very great while to a man that admires a fine woman as much as I do.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: You're an absolute courtier, Sir Sampson.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Not at all, madam. Odsbud, you wrong me; I am not so old neither to be a bare courtier, only a man of words. Odd, I have warm blood about me yet, I can serve a lady any way. Come, come, let me tell you, you women think a man old too soon, faith and troth you so. Come, don't despise fifty; odd, fifty, in a hale constitution, is no such contemptible age.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Fifty a contemptible age! Not at all, a very fashionable age I think. I assure you I know very considerable beaus that set a good face upon fifty. Fifty! I have seen fifty in a side-box by candle-light out-blossom five and twenty.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: O pox, outsides, outsides, a pise take 'em, mere outsides. Hang your side-box beaus; no, I'm none of those, none of your forced trees that pretend to blossom in the fall, and bud when they should bring forth fruit. I am of a long-lived race, and inherit vigour. None of my family married till fifty, yet they begot sons and daughters till four-score. I am of your patriarchs, I, a branch of one of your antediluvian families, fellows that the flood could not wash away. Well, madam, what are your commands? Has any young rogue affronted you, and shall I cut his throat? Or –

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: No, Sir Sampson, I have no quarrel upon my hands. I have more occasion for your conduct than your courage at this time. To tell you the truth, I'm weary of living single, and want a husband.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p:
Odsbud, and 'tis a pity you should.
[Aside] Odd, would she would like me, then I should hamper my young rogues. Odd, would she would; faith and troth she's devilish handsome. (Aloud) Madam, you deserve a good husband, and 'twere a pity you should be thrown away upon any of these young idle rogues about the town. Odd, there's ne'er a young fellow worth hanging, that is, a very young fellow.
