Pise on 'em, they never think beforehand of anything; and if they commit matrimony, 'tis as they commit murder, out of a frolic: and are ready to hang themselves, or to be hanged by the law, the next morning. Odso, have a care, madam.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Therefore I ask your advice, Sir Sampson. I have fortune enough to make any man easy that I can like, if there were such a thing as a young agreeable man, with a reasonable stock of good nature and sense –for I would neither have an absolute wit nor a fool.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Odd, you are hard to please, madam. To find a young fellow that is neither a wit in his own eye nor a fool in the eye of the world is a very hard task. But, faith and troth, you speak very discreetly; for I hate both a wit and a fool.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: She that marries a fool, Sir Sampson, commits the reputation of her honesty or understanding to the censure of the world. And she that marries a very witty man submits both to the severity and insolent conduct of her husband. I should like a man of wit for a lover, because I would have such an one in my power; but I would no more be his wife than his enemy. For his malice is not a more terrible consequence of his aversion than his jealousy is of his love.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: None of old Foresight's sybils ever uttered such a truth. Odsbud, you have won my heart. I hate a wit. I had a son that was spoiled among 'em; a good hopeful lad, till he learned to be a wit –and might have risen in the state –But a pox on't, his wit run him out of his money, and now his poverty has run him out of his wits.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Sir Sampson, as your friend I must tell you you are very much abused in that matter. He's no more mad than you are.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: How, madam? Would I could prove it.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I can tell you how that may be done. But it is a thing that would make me appear to be too much concerned in your affairs.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: [aside] Odsbud, I believe she likes me. (Aloud) Ah, madam, all my affairs are scarce worthy to be laid at your feet; and I wish, madam, they stood in a better posture, that I might make a more becoming offer to a lady of your incomparable beauty and merit. If I had Peru in one hand, and Mexico in t'other, and the Eastern empire under my feet, it would make me only a more glorious victim to be offered at the shrine of your beauty.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Bless me, Sir Sampson, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Odd, madam, I love you. And if you would take my advice in a husband –

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Hold, hold, Sir Sampson. I asked your advice for a husband, and you are giving me your consent. I was indeed thinking to propose something like it in a jest, to satisfy you about Valentine. For if a match were seemingly carried on, between you and me, it would oblige him to throw off his disguise of madness, in apprehension of losing me. For you know he has long pretended a passion for me.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Gadzooks, a most ingenious contrivance, if we were to go through with it. But why must the match only be seemingly carried on? Odd, let it be a real contract.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: O fie, Sir Sampson, what would the world say?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Say? They would say you were a wise woman, and I a happy man. Odd, madam, I'll love you as long as I live, and leave you a good jointure when I die.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Ay, but that is not in your power, Sir Sampson; for when Valentine confesses himself in his senses, he must make over his inheritance to his younger brother.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Odd, you're cunning, a wary baggage! Faith and troth, I like you the better. But I warrant you, I have a proviso in the obligation in favour of myself. Body o' me I have a trick to turn the settlement upon the issue male of our two bodies begotten. Odsbud, let us find children, and I'll find an estate.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Will you? Well, do you find the estate, and leave the other to me.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: O rogue! But I'll trust you. And will you consent? Is it a match then?

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Let me consult my lawyer concerning this obligation, and if I find what you propose practicable, I'll give you my answer.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: With all my heart. Come in with me and I'll lend you the bond. You shall consult your lawyer and I'll consult a parson. Odzooks, I'm a young man. Odzooks I'm a young man, and I'll make it appear. Odd, you're devilish handsome. Faith and troth, you're very handsome, and I'm very young, and very lusty. Odsbud, hussy, you know how to choose, and so do I. Odd, I think we are very well met: Give me your hand, odd, let me kiss it. 'Tis as warm and as soft –as what? Odd, as t'other hand. Give me t'other hand, and I'll mumble 'em, and kiss 'em till they melt in my mouth.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Hold, Sir Sampson, you're profuse of your vigour before your time. You'll spend your estate before you come to it.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: No, no, only give you a rent-roll of my possessions. Ah, baggage! I warrant you for little Sampson. Odd, Sampson's a very good name for an able fellow. Your Sampsons were strong dogs from the beginning.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Have a care, and don't over-act your part. If you remember, the strongest Sampson of your name pulled an old house over his head at last.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Say you so, hussy? Come, let's go then. Odd, I long to be pulling down too; come away. Odso, here's somebody coming.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Is not that she, gone out just now?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Ay, sir, she's just going to the place of appointment. Ah sir, if you are not very faithful and close in this business, you'll certainly be the death of a person that has a most extraordinary passion for your honour's service.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay, who's that?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Even my unworthy self, sir. Sir, I have had an appetite to be fed with your commands a great while. And now, sir, my former master having much troubled the fountain of his understanding, it is a very plausible occasion for me to quench my thirst at the spring of your bounty. I thought I could not recommend myself better to you, sir, than by the delivery of a great beauty and fortune into your arms, whom I have heard you sigh for.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: I'll make thy fortune; say no more. Thou art a pretty fellow, and canst carry a message to a lady in a pretty soft kind of phrase, and with a good persuading accent.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Sir, I have the seeds of rhetoric and oratory in my head. I have been at Cambridge.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay. 'Tis well enough for a servant to be bred at an university, but the education is a little too pedantic for a gentleman. I hope you are secret in your nature, private, close, ha?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: O sir, for that sir, 'tis my chief talent. I'm as secret as the head of Nilus.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay? Who's he, tho'? A Privy Counsellor?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: [aside] O ignorance! (Aloud) A cunning Egyptian, sir, that with his arms would overrun the country, yet nobody could ever find out his headquarters.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Close dog! A good whoremaster, I warrant him. The time draws nigh, Jeremy. Angelica will veiled like a nun, and I must be hooded like a friar. Ha, Jeremy?

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Ay, sir, hooded like a hawk, to seize at first sight upon the quarry. It is the whim of my master's madness to be so dressed. And she is so in love with him, she'll comply with any thing to please him. Poor lady, I'm sure she'll have reason to pray for me, when she finds what a happy exchange she has made, between a madman and so accomplished a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay, faith, so she will, Jeremy. You're a good friend to her, poor creature. I swear I do it hardly so much in consideration of myself as compassion to her.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: 'Tis an act of charity, sir, to save a fine woman with thirty thousand pound from throwing herself away.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: So 'tis, faith. I might have saved several others in my time. But i'Gad I could never find in my heart to marry anybody before.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Well, sir, I'll go and tell her my master's coming, and meet you in half a quarter of an hour, with your disguise, at your own lodgings. You must talk a little madly, she won't distinguish the tone of your voice.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: No, no, let me alone for a counterfeit. I'll be ready for you.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: O Mr Tattle, are you here! I'm glad I have found you. I have been looking up and down for you like any thing, till I'm as tired as any thing in the world.

p.seg: O pox, how shall I get rid of this foolish girl?

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Oh I have pure news, I can tell you pure news. I must not marry the seaman now –my father says so. Why won't you be my husband? You say you love me, and you won't be my husband. And I know you may be my husband now if you please.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: O fie, Miss. Who told you so, child?

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Why, my father. I told him that you loved me.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: O fie, Miss, why did you do so? And who told you so, child?

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Who? Why, you did, did not you?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: O pox, that was yesterday, Miss, that was a great while ago, child. I have been asleep since; slept a whole night, and did not so much as dream of the matter.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Pshaw! Oh, but I dreamt that it was so, tho'.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay, but your father will tell you that dreams come by contraries, child. O fie! What, we must not love one another now. Pshaw! That would be a foolish thing indeed. Fie, fie, you're a woman now, and must think of a new man every morning, and forget him every night. No, no, to marry is to be a child again, and play with the same rattle always. O fie, marrying is a paw thing.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: Well, but don't you love me as well as you did last night then?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: No, no, child, you would not have me.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: No? yes, but I would, tho'.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Pshaw, but tell you, you would not. You forget you're a woman, and don't know your own mind.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: But here's my father, and he knows my mind.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Oh, Mr Tattle, your servant; you are a close man. But methinks your love to my daughter was a secret I might have been trusted with. Or had you a mind to try if I could discover it by my art, hum, ha? I think there is something in your physiognomy that has a resemblance of her, and the girl is like me.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: [aside] And so you would infer that you and I are alike. What does the old prig mean? I'll banter him, and laugh at him, and leave him. (Aloud) I fancy you have a wrong notion of faces.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How? What? A wrong notion? How so?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: In the way of art. I have some taking features, not obvious to vulgar eyes, that are indications of a sudden turn of good fortune in the lottery of wives, and promise a great beauty and great fortune reserved alone for me by a private intrigue of destiny, kept secret from the piercing eye of perspicuity, from all astrologers, and the stars themselves.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How? I will make it appear that what you say is impossible.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Sir, I beg your pardon, I'm in haste.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: For what?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: To be married, sir, married.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Ay, but pray take me along with you, sir.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: No, sir, 'tis to be done privately. I never make confidants.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Well, but my consent I mean. You won't marry my daughter without my consent?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Who, I sir? I'm an absolute stranger to you and your daughter, sir.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Hey-day! What time of the moon is this?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Very true, sir, and desire to continue so. I have no more love for your daughter than I have likeness be glad to know, and shan't know; and yet you shall know it too, and be sorry for't afterwards. I'd have you to know, sir, that I am as knowing as the stars and as secret as the night. And I'm going to be married just now, yet did not know of it half an hour ago, and the lady stays for me, and does not know of it yes. There's a mystery for you. I know you love to untie difficulties. Or if you can't solve this, stay here a quarter of an hour, and I'll come and explain it to you.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: O father, why will you let him go? Won't you make him be my husband?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Mercy on us, what do these lunacies portend? Alas, he's mad, child, stark wild.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: What, and must not I have e'er a husband then? What, must I go to bed to nurse again, and be a child as long as she's an old woman? Indeed but I won't. For now my mind is set upon a man, I will have a man some way or other. Oh! Methinks I'm would go to sleep all my life. For when I'm awake, it makes me wish and long, and I don't know for what. And I'd rather be always a sleeping than sick with thinking.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: O fearful! I think the girl's influenced too. Hussy, you shall have a rod.

sp.speaker: Miss Prue
sp.p: A fiddle of a rod, I'll have a husband, and if you won't get me one, I'll get one for myself. I'll marry our Robin the butler; he says he loves me, and he's a handsome man, and shall be my husband. I warrant he'll be my husband and thank me too, for he told me so.

div2.stage: Enter Scandal, Mrs Foresight, and Nurse.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Did he so? I'll dispatch him for't presently. Rogue! O nurse, come hither.

sp.speaker: Nurse
sp.p: What is your worship's pleasure?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Here, take your young mistress and lock her up presently, till farther orders from me. Not a word, hussy. Do what I bid you, no reply, away! And bid Robin make ready to give an account of his plate and linen, d'ye hear, be gone when I bid you.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: What's the matter, husband?

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: 'Tis not convenient to tell you now. Mr Scandal, heav'n keep us all in our senses. I fear there is a contagious frenzy abroad. How does Valentine?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Oh, I hope he will do well again. I have a message from him to your niece Angelica.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I think she has not returned since she went abroad with Sir Sampson.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Here's Mr Benjamin; he can tell us if his father be come home.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Who, father? Ay, he's come home with a vengeance.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Matter! Why, he's mad.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Mercy on us, I was afraid of this.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: And there's the handsome young woman, she as they say Brother Val went mad for, she's mad too, I think.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: O my poor niece, my poor niece, is she gone too? Well, I shall run mad next.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Well, but how mad? How d'ye mean?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Nay, I'll give you leave to guess. I'll undertake to make a voyage to Antegoa. No, hold, I mayn't say so neither –but I'll sail as far as Ligorn and back again before you shall guess at the matter, and do nothing else. Mess, you may take in all the points of the compass and not hit right.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Your experiment will take up a little too much time.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why, then I'll tell you, there's a new wedding upon the stocks, and they two are a going to be married to rights.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why father and –the young woman. I can't hit of her name.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Angelica?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Ay, the same.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Sir Sampson and Angelica? Impossible!

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: That may be, but I'm sure it is as I tell you.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: 'S'death, it's a jest. I can't believe it.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Look you, friend, it's nothing to me, whether you believe it or no. What I say is true, d'ye see? They are married, or just going to be marries, I know not which.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Well, but they are not mad, that is, not lunatic?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: I don't know what you may call madness, but she's mad for a husband, and he's horn mad, I think, or they'd ne'er make a match together. Here they come.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Sampson, Angelica, with Buckram.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Where is this old soothsayer? This uncle of mine elect? Aha, old Foresight, uncle Foresight, wish me joy uncle Foresight, double joy, both as uncle and astrologer. Here's a conjunction that was not foretold in all your Ephemeris. The brightest star in the blue firmament is 'shot from above in a jelly of love', and so forth; and I'm lord of the ascendant. Odd, you're an old fellow, Foresight –uncle I mean, a very old fellow, uncle Foresight; and yet you shall live to dance at my wedding, faith and troth you shall. Odd, we'll have the music of the spheres for thee, old Lilly, that we will, and thou shalt lead up a dance in via Lactea.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: I'm thunder-strook! You are not married to my niece?

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Not absolutely married, uncle, but very near it, within a kiss of the matter, as you see.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: 'Tis very true indeed, uncle. I hope you'll be my father, and give me.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: That he shall, or I'll burn his globes. Body o' me, he shall be thy father, I'll make him thy father, and thou shalt make me a father, and I'll make thee a mother, and we'll beget sons and daughters enough to put the weekly bills out of countenance.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Death and hell! Where's Valentine?

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: This is so surprising –

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: How! What does my aunt say? Surprising, aunt? Not at all, for a young couple to make a match in winter? Not at all. It's a plot to undermine cold weather, and destroy that usurper of a bed called a warming-pan.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: I'm glad to hear you have so much fire in you, Sir Sampson.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Mess, I fear his fire's little better than tinder. Mayhap it will only serve to light up a match for somebody else. The young woman's a handsome young woman, I can't deny it. But, father, if I might be your pilot in this case, you should not marry her. It's just the same thing as if so be you should sail so far as the Straits without provision.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Who gave you authority to speak, sirrah? To your element, fish, be mute, fish, and to sea. Rule your helm, sirrah, don't direct me.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Well, well, take you care of your own helm, or you mayn't keep your own vessel steady.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Why, you impudent tarpaulin! Sirrah, do you bring your forecastle jest upon your father? But I shall be even with you, I won't give you a groat. Mr Buckram, is he conveyance so worded that nothing can possibly descend to this scoundrel? I would not so much as have him have the prospect of an estate, tho' there were no way to come to it but by the north-east passage.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Sir, it is drawn according to your directions; there is not the least cranny of the law unstopped.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Lawyer, I believe there's many a cranny and leak unstopped in your conscience. If so be that one had a pump to your bosom, I believe we should discover a foul hold. They say a witch will sail in a sieve. But I believe the devil would not venture aboard o'your conscience. And that's for you.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Hold your tongue, sirrah. How now, who's there?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Oh, sister, the most unlucky accident!

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Oh, the two most unfortunate poor creatures in the world we are!

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Bless us! How so?

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Ah Mr Tattle and I, poor Mr Tattle and I are –I can't speak it out.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Nor I. But poor Mrs Frail and I are –

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: Married.

sp.speaker: Mrs Foresight
sp.p: Married! How?

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Suddenly –before we knew where we were –that villain Jeremy, by the help of disguises, tricked us into one another.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Why, you told me just now you went hence in haste to be married.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: But I believe Mr Tattle meant the favour to me, I thank him.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: I did, as hope to be saved, madam, my intentions were good. But this is the most cruel thing, to marry one does not know how, nor why, nor wherefore. The devil take me if ever I was so much concerned at anything in my life.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: 'Tis very unhappy, if you don't care for one another.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: The least in the world. That is for my part, I speak for myself. Gad, I never had the least thought of serious kindness. I never liked anybody less in my life. Poor woman! Gad, I'm sorry for her too, for I have no reason to hate her neither; but I believe I shall lead her a damned sort of a life.

p.seg: He's better than no husband at all, tho' he's a coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: [to her] Ay, ay, it's well it's no worse. (Aloud) Nay, for my part I always despised Mr Tattle of all things. Nothing but his being my husband could have made me like him less.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Look you there, I thought as much. Pox on't, I wish we could keep it secret. Why, I don't believe any of this company would speak of it.

sp.speaker: Mrs Frail
sp.p: But, my dear, that's impossible. The parson and that rogue Jeremy will publish it.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Ay, my dear, so they will, as you say.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Oh, you'll agree very well in a little time. Custom will make it easy to you.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: Easy! Pox on't, I don't believe I shall sleep tonight.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Sleep, quotha? No, why, you would not sleep o'your wedding night? I'm an older fellow than you and don't mean to sleep.

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Why there's another match now, as thof a couple of privateers were looking for a prize, and should fall foul of one another. I'm sorry for the young man with all my heart. Look you, friend, if I may advise you, when she's going (for that you must expect, I have experience of her), when she's going, let her go. For no matrimony is tough enough to hold her, and if she can't drag anchor along with her, she'll breal her cable, I can tell you that. Who's here, the madman?

div2.stage: Enter Valentine dressed, Scandal and Jeremy.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: No here's the fool, and if occasion be, I'll give it under my hand.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: How now?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Sir, I'm come to acknowledge my errors, and ask your pardon.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: What, have you found your senses at last, then? In good time, sir.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: You were abused, sir, I never was distracted.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: How? Not mad, Mr Scandal?

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: No, really, sir; I'm his witness, it was all counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I thought I had reasons. But it was a poor contrivance, the effect has shewn it such.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Contrivance! What, to cheat me? To cheat your father? Sirrah, could you hope to prosper?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Indeed, I thought, sir, when the father endeavoured to undo the son, it was a reasonable return of nature.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Very good, sir. Mr Buckram, are you ready? Come, sir, will you sign and seal?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: If you please, sir. But first I would ask this lady one question.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Sir, you must ask my leave first. That lady? No, sir, you shall ask that lady no questions till you have asked her blessing, sir. That lady is to be my wife.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I have heard as much, sir, but I would have it from her own mouth.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: That's as much as to say, I lie, sir, and you don't believe what I say.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Pardon me, sir. But I reflect that I very lately counterfeited madness. I don't know but the frolic may go round.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Come, chuck, satisfy him, answer him. Come, come, Mr Buckram, the pen and ink.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Here it is, sir, with the deed, all is ready.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: 'Tis true, you have a great while pretended love to me; nay, what if you were sincere? Still you must pardon me if I think my own inclinations have a better right to dispose of my person than yours.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Are you answered now, sir?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Where's your plot, sir, and your contrivance now, sir? Will you sign, sir? Come will you sign and seal?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: With all my heart, sir.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: 'S'death, you are not mad indeed, to ruin yourself?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I have been disappointed of my only hope, and he that loses hope may part with any thing. I never valued fortune but as it was subservient to my pleasure, and my only pleasure was to please this lady. I have made many vain attempts, and find at last that nothing but my ruin can effect it, which for that reason I will sign to. Give me the paper.

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Here is the deed, sir.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: But where is the bond by which I am obliged to sign this?

sp.speaker: Buckram
sp.p: Sir Sampson, you have it.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: No, I have it. And I'll use it, as I would every thing that is an enemy to Valentine.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: How now?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: [to Valentine] Had I the world to give you, it could not make me worthy of so generous and faithful a passion. Here's my hand, my heart was always yours, and struggled very hard to make this utmost trial of your virtue.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Between pleasure and amazement I am lost. But on my knees I take the blessing.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ouns, what is the meaning of this?

sp.speaker: Ben
sp.p: Mess, here's the wind changed again. Father, you and I may make a voyage together now.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Well, Sir Sampson, since I have played you a trick, I'll advise you how you may avoid such another. Learn to be a good father, or you'll never get a second wife. I always loved your son, and hated your unforgiving nature. I was resolved to try him to the utmost. I have tried you too, and know you both. You have not more faults than he has virtues, and 'tis hardly more pleasure to me that I can make him and myself happy than that I can punish you.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: If my happiness could receive addition, this kind surprise would make it double.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: Ouns, you're a crocodile.

sp.speaker: Foresight
sp.p: Really, Sir Sampson, this is a sudden eclipse.

sp.speaker: Sir Sampson
sp.p: You're an illiterate fool, and I'm another, and the stars are liars, and if I had breath enough, I'd curse them and you, myself and everybody. Ouns! Cullied, bubbled, jilted, woman-bobbed at last –I have not patience.

sp.speaker: Tattle
sp.p: If the gentleman is in this disorder for want of a wife, I can spare him mine. [To Jeremy] Oh, are you there, sir? I'm indebted to you for my happiness.

sp.speaker: Jeremy
sp.p: Sir, I ask you ten thousand pardons, 'twas an errant mistake. You see, sir, my master was never mad, or anything like it. Then how could it be otherwise?

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Tattle, I thank you, you would have interposed between me and heaven, but Providence laid Purgatory in your way. You have but justice.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: I hear the fiddles that Sir Sampson provided for his own wedding. Methinks 'tis pity they should not be employed when the match is so much mended. Valentine, tho' it be morning, we may have a dance.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Anything, my friend, everything that looks like joy and transport.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p: Call 'em, Jeremy.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: I have done dissembling now, Valentine, and if that coldness which I have always worn before you should turn to an extreme fondness, you must suspect it.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: I'll prevent that suspicion, for I intend to dote on at that immoderate rate, that your fondness shall never distinguish itself enough to be taken notice of. If ever you seem to love too much, it must be only when I can't love enough.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: Have a care of large promises; you know you are apt to run more in debt than you are able (to) pay.

sp.speaker: Valentine
sp.p: Therefore I yield my body as your prisoner, and make your best on't.

sp.speaker: Scandal
sp.p:
The music stays for you. Dance
Well, madam, you have done exemplary justice, in punishing an inhumane father and rewarding a faithful lover. But there is a third good work, which I, in particular, must thank you for. I was an infidel to your sex, and you have converted me. For now I am convinced that all women are not like fortune, blind in bestowing favours, either on those who do not merit, or who do not want 'em.

sp.speaker: Angelica
sp.p: 'Tis an unreasonable accusation that you lay upon our sex. You tax us with injustice, only to cover your own want of merit. You would all have the reward of love, but few have the constancy to stay till it becomes your due. Men are generally hypocrites and infidels. They pretend to worship, but have neither zeal nor faith. How few, like Valentine, would persevere even unto martyrdom, and sacrifice their interest to their constancy. In admiring me you misplace the novelty.

lg.l: The miracle today is that we find
A lover true, not that a woman's kind.
